summary: Specifies the Group Secure Association Key Management Protocol, a framework for creating and managing cryptographic groups. It spreads group policy, authenticates members, makes access-control decisions, recovers from compromised members, lets group-security duties be delegated, and generates group keys. It is a standards-track protocol.

eli5.summary: Imagine a secret treehouse club. One protocol decides who may join, hands out the secret password, changes the password if someone leaks it, and can close the club down when it is over.

questions: how to manage keys for secure multicast
how does group key management work
what is a group controller key server
subtitle: How a secure group gets its policy, its members and its shared keys, and how it recovers when a member goes bad.

tldr.problem: A cryptographic group, where many parties share a key, needs a way to agree on a security policy, check who may join, hand out keys safely and recover when a member is compromised.
tldr.mechanism: A Group Owner signs a policy token. A Group Controller Key Server enforces it, admitting members through a signed join exchange (Request to Join, Key Download, Acknowledgement) and later rekeying or destroying the group with signed Rekey Event messages.
tldr.outcome: GSAKMP is a Proposed Standard. It supplies the protocol, a default Security Suite 1 and IANA registries, and it scales out by delegating work to subordinate key servers.

today: RFC 4535 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its companion policy token format is defined in RFC 4534.

sections.title: What GSAKMP Is For
sections.content:
GSAKMP provides policy distribution, policy enforcement, key distribution and key management for cryptographic groups, sets of entities that share a common key or set of keys. For a group to perform security services it needs a Group Secure Association (GSA): a shared, group-level definition of security policy plus enforcement of it. Handing out keys is the mechanism that enforces the access control policy.

The security features of the establishment protocol are group policy identification, group policy dissemination, security association establishment between each member and the key server to protect data, and access control checking. Every party's identity MUST be asserted and authenticated, and each MUST be verified as authorized for its role.

GSAKMP builds group creation and management, but other protocols handle the rest. A small video conference might use SIP to announce its time and formats, and a large transmission might use a multicast announcement protocol. The document derives from ISAKMP and FIPS Pub 196, and conforms to the IETF MSEC architecture.
sections.eli5: A club needs rules, a way to check who is allowed in, and a secret password. GSAKMP handles all three, but it does not tell the club what to do once everyone is inside.

sections.title: Roles and the Trust Model
sections.content:
Trust flows from one source. The GSAKMP trust model has four components, and every security-relevant decision is traceable to the Group Owner (GO) and to the PKI root that lets members verify the GO.

  • Group Owner (GO): creates the policy, writes it into a policy token and signs it.
  • Group Controller Key Server (GC/KS): creates and distributes keys, rekeys the group, manages membership and enforces the policy token when admitting members.
  • Subordinate GC/KS (S-GC/KS): has all of the GC/KS's authority except creating the group traffic key, so work can be spread across many nodes.
  • Group Member (GM): checks that every security-relevant action is authorized and uses the keys properly.

The policy token carries identification, access control rules (who may hold the keys), authorization rules (who may be an S-GC/KS) and the mechanisms the group uses, and it is a CMS signed object. A joining member accepts the group only if the token verifies, the GC/KS is an authorized disseminator, and the group mechanisms are acceptable for protecting its data.

GSAKMP offers three speaker configurations: one authorized speaker (the default, which implementations MUST support), all members as speakers (MUST be supported, but with no per-sender anti-replay sequence checking), or a chosen subset with separate state per speaker (MAY be supported, and does not scale to many speakers). The trust model assumes the GC/KS and GO are never compromised.
sections.eli5: The club owner writes the rules and signs them. A door keeper checks the rules and gives out the password. Helpers can hand out passwords too, but only the main door keeper makes the password.

sections.title: Joining a Group
sections.content:
Group establishment uses three mandatory messages. A potential member sends a Request to Join (RTJ, exchange type 8). The GC/KS checks the header and group ID, extracts the sender's identity, checks access control and verifies the signature. It replies with a Key Download (type 9) signed by the GC/KS. This holds the member's identity, key creation material, and the policy token and key data encrypted in a key encryption key (KEK) derived from the key creation material. The member verifies the freshness values and signature, decrypts and checks the policy token, then confirms both the GO and the GC/KS are authorized. It finishes with a signed Key Download Ack/Failure (type 4).

Two optional messages exist. The Request to Join Error (type 11) is deliberately unsigned, because the member does not yet know who may act as GC/KS and signing every denial would invite denial of service. The Lack of Ack (type 12) warns a member of eviction if no valid acknowledgement arrives. Using only the mandatory messages is Terse Mode (MUST be supported); adding the error messages is Verbose Mode (MAY).

Freshness comes from nonces unless synchronized time is available. If no response comes, the GM SHOULD resend the RTJ up to three times, and a GC/KS MUST process no more than one valid RTJ per member per group at a time. In an optional receive-only mode, the key server just sends a Key Download after an out-of-band event and no RTJ or acknowledgement is used.
sections.eli5: You knock and show your badge. The door keeper checks it, then slips you a sealed envelope with the rules and password. You open it, check the rules, and tell the door keeper you got it.

sections.title: Cookies, Assumptions and Attack Defenses
sections.content:
Among the security assumptions: the platform separates processes and data, key generation yields strong keys, random values come from a strong or properly seeded source, and system clocks are close to correct. The allowed clock skew across the group is policy configurable, with a default of 5 minutes. Replays are defeated by signed nonces. GSAKMP does not provide identity protection and does not secure the group's multicast routing, so a rogue member or outsider might direct multicast flooding at a victim. If the GO is compromised the group must end; if an S-GC/KS is compromised its members must re-register. Members spot this by finding the certificate on a CRL.

For denial of service defense, the optional cookie exchange protects a GC/KS from floods of Request to Join messages from forged addresses. In cookie mode the GC/KS SHOULD reject an RTJ with no cookie and instead send a Cookie Download (type 10). The member must retry with that cookie. The RFC gives an example cookie, a secret version number plus a hash of the member's nonce, its IP address and a secret that the server changes often, so the server needs no saved state until the member proves it can receive at its claimed address.

Diffie-Hellman exponents MUST NOT be derived from long-lived secrets, and rekey messages need high availability: implementations that support rekey MUST support retransmitting them.
sections.eli5: If a crowd of pranksters knocks all at once, the door keeper first hands each knocker a numbered ticket and asks them to come back with it. Only people who really got the ticket can continue.

sections.title: Rekeying, Eviction and Leaving
sections.content:
A rekey event is any action, such as a compromise report or key expiration, that needs a new group key or rekey information. The GC/KS MUST send a signed Rekey Event message (type 5) carrying the new group traffic protection key (GTPK) and rekey information. Members MUST discard it if the signature fails, and a new policy token sent in it MUST be encrypted in the old GTPK. Policy updates also travel in Rekey Events, and group destruction is a Rekey Event whose Sequence ID is 0xFFFFFFFF.

Rekeying can use Logical Key Hierarchy (LKH), which is optional, since sometimes it is better to destroy a compromised group and rebuild it. To evict a member, the group rekeys so its keys no longer work. To bar it for good, the policy token's rules MUST be updated to exclude it.

A member may leave quietly by deleting its keys if membership carries no cost, otherwise it SHOULD de-register. That is a three-message exchange: Request to Depart (type 13), Departure Response (14) and Departure Ack (15). GC/KS implementations MUST support it. A GM that sends no acknowledgement of its Key Download is evicted at the next policy-defined Rekey Event.

For large groups, S-GC/KSes run largely self-contained sub-groups. The primary GC/KS multicasts Rekey Events to its S-GC/KSes, and each forwards its own to its sub-group, with a key tree independent of the primary one. An S-GC/KS that sees a member to expel asks the GC/KS, which gets a new policy token from the GO listing that member as excluded.
sections.eli5: When someone leaks the password, the door keeper announces a new one, but only to people still trusted. Members who want to quit can say goodbye properly, and the club can also be closed with one last message.

sections.title: Headers, Payloads and Security Suite 1
sections.content:
Every message is a GSAKMP header followed by chained payloads, and each payload names the type of the next. The header holds a group ID (type, length and value), Next Payload, Version (currently 1), Exchange Type, a 4-octet Sequence ID and a 4-octet Length. Group ID types include UTF-8, octet string (MUST be implemented), IPv4 and IPv6, and the value SHOULD include a random element of at least eight octets. The Sequence ID guards group management messages against replay: it starts at 1, increases with each such message, and receivers must see it grow. Multi-octet integers use network byte order, and padding MUST NOT be used.

Payload types are Policy Token, Key Download Packet, Rekey Event, Identification, Certificate, Signature, Notification, Vendor ID, Key Creation and Nonce.

Security Suite 1 MUST be supported. GSAKMP does not negotiate algorithms: the GO sets them in the policy token. Suite 1 uses AES in CBC mode with 128-bit keys for key download and policy token encryption, DSS with SHA-1 for signatures and nonce hashing, and Diffie-Hellman with the second Oakley group from IKE (g of 2, a 1024-bit prime). Other suites MAY be defined.
sections.eli5: Every message begins with a label saying which club it is for and what kind of message it is, with a counter so old messages cannot be replayed. The default secret code is already chosen so everyone can start.

sections.title: State Diagram and IANA
sections.content:
The state diagram has five states. Idle is where an application waits. A key server moves to Wait for GC/KS Event when told to create a group, then to Wait for Response from Key Download after a valid RTJ. A member moves to Wait for Group Membership on a join command, and to Wait for Group Membership Event once it has sent its acknowledgement and holds the key. Errors, timeouts and delete commands return participants to Idle.

IANA assigned GSAKMP port 3761 in both the UDP and TCP spaces, and implementations MUST use it. The RFC creates registries for group ID types, payload types, exchange types, policy token types, key download item types, rekey event types, notification types and others. Most changes need IETF Standards Action; cryptographic key, identification, certificate, signature, nonce hash and key creation types need only Expert Review. An appendix covers LKH and gives examples of LKH key download and rekey.
sections.eli5: Each helper is always in one mood at a time: waiting, answering a knock, or waiting for news. Particular events nudge them from one mood to the next.

messages.label: Request to Join
messages.note: Mandatory. Carries key creation material, a nonce and the member's signature.

messages.label: Key Download
messages.note: Mandatory. Signed; holds the encrypted policy token and keys.

messages.label: Lack of Ack
messages.note: Optional, Verbose Mode. Warns of eviction if no valid ack arrives.

items.label: Key Download Ack/Failure
items.desc: Member reports the status of the key download.

items.label: Rekey Event
items.desc: New keys, policy updates and group destruction.

items.label: Request to Join
items.desc: Member asks the GC/KS for admission.

items.label: Key Download
items.desc: GC/KS sends the policy token and keys.

items.label: Lack of Ack
items.desc: Optional warning that no acknowledgement arrived.

viz.caption: WHO DOES WHAT IN A GSAKMP GROUP

items.title: Group Owner
items.text: Writes and signs the policy token.

items.title: GC/KS
items.text: Creates keys, admits members, rekeys the group.

items.title: Subordinate GC/KS
items.text: Shares the load but never creates the group traffic key.

items.title: Group Member
items.text: Verifies every action is authorized and protects the keys.
